opening: A game with piles of stones whose winner can be read off from the binary digits of the pile sizes.

steps.prompt: The game: several piles of stones; a move removes any positive number of stones from a single pile; whoever takes the last stone wins. With two piles of 6 and 6, who wins?
options: The second player, by copying each move in the other pile
It depends on the first move
nudges: Whatever the first player does to one pile, what can the second do to the other?
steps.showed: Equal piles are lost for the player to move.

steps.prompt: Same game with piles of 1, 2 and 3. Who wins with perfect play?
nudges: Try each first move. Can the second player always leave two equal piles (and nothing else)?
steps.showed: Every first move can be answered by leaving two equal piles.

nudges: In binary, how many of 1, 2, 3 have a 1 in the 1s place, and how many in the 2s place?
steps.showed: Zero. And 6 XOR 6 is also zero. Both were lost positions for the player to move.
Not zero, so perhaps this position is good for the player to move.

steps.prompt: From piles 3, 4, 5, the player to move wants to leave piles whose XOR is 0 by reducing one pile. What are the three pile sizes afterwards?
nudges: The XOR is 2. Which pile becomes smaller when you XOR it with 2?
steps.showed: Reduce the 3 to 3 XOR 2 = 1. The other piles would grow if XORed with 2, which is not allowed.

steps.prompt: The piles have XOR 0 and you must move. Can your move leave XOR 0 again?
options: No: changing one pile changes the total XOR
Yes, by taking an even number of stones
Yes, if two piles are equal
nudges: If only one pile changes from $p$ to $q$, what is the new XOR in terms of the old one?
steps.showed: From XOR 0 you are forced to hand over a non-zero XOR.

steps.prompt: The piles have XOR $X \ne 0$. Is there always a pile $p$ with $p$ XOR $X$ smaller than $p$?
options: Yes: any pile that has a 1 in the highest binary place of $X$
Only if some pile is larger than $X$
nudges: Look at the highest place where $X$ has a 1. Does some pile have a 1 there? What happens to that pile when XORed with $X$?
steps.showed: That place is 1 in an odd number of piles, so in at least one. XOR with $X$ turns it to 0 and only changes lower places, so the pile gets smaller.

steps.prompt: Piles of 7, 9, 12 and 14. How many different winning first moves are there?
nudges: What is the XOR of the four piles, and which piles have a 1 in its highest place?
steps.showed: The XOR is 12, whose highest place is the 8s place. Piles 9, 12 and 14 have it: reduce 9 to 5, or 12 to 0, or 14 to 2.

steps.prompt: Piles of 5, 5, 7, 7 and 9. How many stones should the first player take?
nudges: Which piles already cancel each other?
steps.showed: The pairs cancel; remove the odd pile out entirely and copy from then on.

steps.prompt: In the game above, prove that if the XOR of all pile sizes is 0, then after any move it is not 0.
claims: A move changes exactly one pile, from p to some q with q < p; all other piles stay the same.
The new XOR equals the old XOR, XOR p, XOR q (remove the old pile, put in the new one), which is 0 XOR p XOR q = p XOR q.
p XOR q is 0 only when p = q, and here q < p, so the new XOR is not 0.
nudges: How many piles does a move change?
How do you update a XOR when one of its terms changes?
steps.showed: Swap one term of the XOR for a different one and the total cannot stay 0.

steps.prompt: Piles of 7, 11, 13 and 14 stones; a move removes any positive number from one pile; last stone wins. How many different winning first moves are there?
nudges: What is the XOR of the four piles?
Which piles get smaller when XORed with that value?
steps.showed: The XOR is 15, whose top bit is the 8s place. Exactly the piles with that bit (11, 13, 14) can be lowered to make the XOR 0: to 4, 2 and 1.

steps.prompt: How many sets of three different pile sizes a < b < c, all at most 15, are losing for the player to move?
steps.verify:
import itertools
result = sum(1 for a, b, c in itertools.combinations(range(1, 16), 3) if a ^ b ^ c == 0)
nudges: Once a and b are chosen, how many values of c make the position losing?
Each losing set is found from how many choices of (a, b)?
steps.showed: c must equal a XOR b, which is automatically between 1 and 15 and different from both. There are 15 x 14 / 2 = 105 pairs, and each losing set is produced by 3 of them: 35.

steps.prompt: Reverse the goal: whoever takes the last stone LOSES. With piles of 1, 2 and 3, who wins?
nudges: With piles of 1 and 1, who wins under the reversed goal? And with a single pile of 5?
Can the player with the normal winning strategy keep following it until the position is only piles of size 1 and at most one bigger pile, and then choose how to finish?
steps.showed: Still the second player. Play exactly as in the normal game (keep the XOR at 0) until a move would leave only piles of size 1; at that moment leave an odd number of them instead of an even number. Only positions made entirely of single stones behave differently.

steps.prompt: Now make it run. Write a program for the task below; it is judged on large inputs with a time limit.
steps.showed: One XOR per game. The work is in reading the input format correctly and resetting the XOR for each game.

reveal.name: Nim and the XOR of the piles
reveal.statement: In Nim (take any number from one pile, last stone wins) the player to move loses exactly when the XOR of the pile sizes is 0. From XOR 0 every move makes it non-zero; from XOR $X \ne 0$, reduce a pile $p$ having the top bit of $X$ to $p \oplus X$.
reveal.remark: Many games are Nim in disguise. When a game splits into independent parts, compute a "pile size" for each part by brute force on small cases and XOR them.
